content: Medication, also referred to as medicine or drugs, encompasses any substance or combination of substances administered to humans or animals with the purpose of treating or preventing disease. Additionally, medications may be used to aid in medical diagnosis. Pharmaceutical companies manufacture commercial medications, which are often protected by patents. Once these patents expire, other companies can produce equivalent versions known as generic drugs. Medications can be classified based on their chemical properties, method of administration, or the biological system they affect. A widely recognized classification system is the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) Classification System. Types of Medications For the Gastrointestinal Tract or Digestive System: Upper Digestive Tract: Includes antacids, reflux suppressants, antiflatulents, antidopaminergics, proton pump inhibitors, H2-receptor antagonists, cytoprotectants, and prostaglandin analogues. Lower Digestive Tract: Includes laxatives, antispasmodics, antidiarrhoeals, bile acid sequestrants, and opioids. For the Cardiovascular System: General: Medications include beta-receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics, cardiac glycosides, antiarrhythmics, nitrates, antianginals, vasoconstrictors, vasodilators, and peripheral activators. Blood Pressure Regulation: Includes ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and alpha blockers. Coagulation: Includes anticoagulants, heparin, antiplatelet drugs, fibrinolytics, anti-hemophilic factors, and haemostatic drugs. Atherosclerosis/Cholesterol Management: Includes hypolipidaemic agents and statins. For the Central Nervous System: Medications include hypnotics, anesthetics, antipsychotics, antidepressants (such as tricyclic antidepressants, monoamine oxidase inhibitors, lithium salts, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), antiemetics, anticonvulsants, antiepileptics, anxiolytics, barbiturates, drugs for movement disorders, stimulants (including amphetamines), benzodiazepines, cyclopyrrolones, dopamine antagonists, antihistamines, cholinergics, anticholinergics, emetics, cannabinoids, and 5-HT antagonists. For Pain and Consciousness (Analgesic Drugs): The primary classes of painkillers include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opioids, and other agents such as paracetamol, tricyclic antidepressants, and anticonvulsants. For Musculoskeletal Disorders: Medications include NSAIDs (including COX-2 selective inhibitors), muscle relaxants, neuromuscular drugs, and anticholinesterases. For the Eye: General: Includes adrenergic neuron blockers, astringents, and ocular lubricants. Diagnostic: Includes topical anesthetics, sympathomimetics, parasympatholytics, mydriatics, and cycloplegics. Antibacterial: Includes antibiotics, topical antibiotics, sulfa drugs, aminoglycosides, and fluoroquinolones. Antiviral and Antifungal: Includes imidazoles and polyenes. Anti-inflammatory: Includes NSAIDs and corticosteroids. Anti-allergy: Includes mast cell inhibitors. Anti-glaucoma: Includes adrenergic agonists, beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, hyperosmotics, cholinergics, miotics, parasympathomimetics, prostaglandin agonists, and prostaglandin inhibitors. For the Ear, Nose, and Oropharynx: Medications include sympathomimetics, antihistamines, anticholinergics, NSAIDs, steroids, antiseptics, local anesthetics, antifungals, and cerumenolytics. For the Respiratory System: Medications include bronchodilators, NSAIDs, anti-allergic agents, antitussives, mucolytics, decongestants, corticosteroids, beta-receptor antagonists, anticholinergics, and steroids. For Endocrine Problems: Medications include androgens, antiandrogens, gonadotropins, corticosteroids, growth hormones, insulin, antidiabetics (such as sulfonylureas, biguanides/metformin, thiazolidinediones, and insulin), thyroid hormones, antithyroid drugs, calcitonin, diphosphonates, and vasopressin analogues. For the Reproductive or Urinary System: Medications include antifungals, alkalizing agents, quinolones, antibiotics, cholinergics, anticholinergics, anticholinesterases, antispasmodics, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, selective alpha-1 blockers, and sildenafil. For Contraception: Includes hormonal contraception, ormeloxifene, and spermicides. For Obstetrics and Gynecology: Medications include NSAIDs, anticholinergics, haemostatic drugs, antifibrinolytics, hormone replacement therapy, bone regulators, beta-receptor agonists, follicle-stimulating hormones, luteinizing hormones, LHRH agonists, progestogens, dopamine agonists, estrogens, prostaglandins, gonadorelin, clomiphene, tamoxifen, and diethylstilbestrol. For the Skin: Medications include emollients, antipruritics, antifungals, disinfectants, scabicides, pediculicides, tar products, vitamin A derivatives, vitamin D analogues, keratolytics, abrasives, systemic antibiotics, topical antibiotics, hormones, desloughing agents, exudate absorbents, fibrinolytics, proteolytics, sunscreens, antiperspirants, and corticosteroids. For Infections and Infestations: Medications include antibiotics, antifungals, antileprotic drugs, antituberculous drugs, antimalarials, anthelmintics, amoebicides, antivirals, and antiprotozoals. For Immunology: Medications include vaccines, immunoglobulins, immunosuppressants, interferons, and monoclonal antibodies. For Allergic Disorders: Medications include anti-allergic agents, antihistamines, and NSAIDs. For Nutrition: Medications include tonics, iron preparations, electrolytes, parenteral nutritional supplements, vitamins, anti-obesity drugs, anabolic drugs, haematopoietic drugs, and food product drugs. For Neoplastic Disorders: Medications include cytotoxic drugs, sex hormones, aromatase inhibitors, somatostatin inhibitors, recombinant interleukins, granulocyte colony-stimulating factors (G-CSF), and erythropoietin. For Diagnostics: Contrast media are used. Legal Considerations Medications are categorized as either over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, which are available without special restrictions, or prescription-only medicines (POM), which require a licensed medical practitioner's prescription. The distinction between OTC and prescription drugs varies by legal jurisdiction. The International Narcotics Control Board of the United Nations enforces global regulations prohibiting certain medications, publishing a comprehensive list of restricted chemicals and plants. OTC medications are considered safe for general use when taken as directed. Some countries, such as the United Kingdom, have a third category of pharmacy medicines, which can only be sold in registered pharmacies under a pharmacist's supervision. Naming of Drugs It is often preferable to refer to drugs by their generic names rather than their brand names. Other Related Topics Polypharmacy: Refers to the concurrent use of multiple prescribed and non-prescribed medications (typically five or more), which can lead to adverse effects in patients. Zoopharmacognosy: Describes the use of drugs and non-food substances by animals.
